entry: Heart disease involving reduced blood flow to the cardiac muscle, caused by plaques in the coronary arteries. It is the most common of the [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular diseases]] and the most common cause of death globally: in 2015 it affected 110 million people and caused 8.9 million deaths, or 15.6% of all deaths. Risk factors include [[Hypertension|high blood pressure]], smoking, [[Diabetes|diabetes mellitus]], [[Obesity|obesity]] and high blood cholesterol. Prevention centers on a healthy diet, [[Exercise|exercise]] and a healthy weight; treatment may include medication or procedures such as coronary artery bypass surgery in severe disease.

British television [[Soap opera|soap opera]] created by Granada Television and broadcast since December 9, 1960. Set in the fictional town of Weatherfield in [[Greater Manchester]], it centers on a cobbled terraced street. Influenced by kitchen-sink realism, it portrays a working-class community with humor and relatable characters, and it introduced northern English [[Dialect|dialect]] to British television. In 2010, [[Guinness World Records]] recognized it as the world's longest-running television soap opera. As of 2025 it averages about four million viewers per episode.

Subfamily of enveloped RNA [[Virus|viruses]] in the family Coronaviridae. Coronaviruses infect [[Mammal|mammals]] and birds. In humans, mild varieties cause some cases of the [[Common cold]], while more lethal ones cause SARS, MERS and [[COVID-19]]. In cows and pigs they cause [[Diarrhea]], and in mice they cause [[Hepatitis]] and encephalomyelitis. Their genomes, of 26 to 32 kilobases, are among the largest of any RNA virus. The name derives from Latin *corona*, meaning "crown" or "wreath", for the club-shaped spikes that project from the virus surface and give it a halo-like appearance under electron microscopy. As of 2020, 45 species are officially recognized.

Coastal city in [[Texas]] (pop., 2025: 317,247), county seat and largest city of Nueces County. It is the eighth-most populous city in Texas and lies 130 miles (210 km) southeast of [[San Antonio]] and 208 miles (335 km) southwest of [[Houston]]. Its economy rests on energy, manufacturing, healthcare, tourism and maritime commerce. The Port of Corpus Christi is one of the largest ports in the United States by total waterborne tonnage. Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is one of two U.S. military locations that train primary student pilots.

Collection of Roman legal works, enacted 529–534 by order of [[Justinian I]]. It comprised the *Codex*, a compilation of imperial enactments; the *Digest* or *Pandects*, extracts from the writings of Roman jurists; and the *Institutes*, a student textbook. All three were given force of law and were intended as the sole source of law. Later imperial laws, the *Novellae Constitutiones*, are counted as a fourth part. The work was directed by Tribonian in [[Constantinople]] and composed almost entirely in Latin. Revised into Greek, it formed the basis of Byzantine law through the *Basilika* until the 15th century. Rediscovered in medieval Western Europe, it became the foundation of law in all [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] jurisdictions and influenced the canon law of the [[Catholic Church]]. Its influence on [[Common law]] systems was less marked.

Statistical relationship between two [[Random variable|random variables]], usually a linear one. The most common measure is the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, denoted ρ or r. It is the [[Covariance|covariance]] of two variables divided by the product of their [[Standard deviation|standard deviations]], ranging from −1 to +1. Pearson's coefficient is sensitive only to linear relationships, which may be present even when one variable is a nonlinear function of the other. [[Karl Pearson]] developed it from a similar idea by [[Francis Galton]]. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was developed to be more robust and to detect less structured relationships.

Correlation is not the same as dependence: independent variables are uncorrelated, but uncorrelated variables may still be dependent. A correlation alone does not indicate causation. Correlations are nonetheless useful for prediction; an electric utility, for example, can anticipate lower output on a mild day because demand depends on the weather. The absolute value of Pearson's coefficient cannot exceed 1, a corollary of the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]].

Gradual deterioration of materials, usually [[Metal|metals]], by chemical or electrochemical reaction with their environment. In its most common form, a metal is oxidized by an oxidant such as [[Oxygen]] or hydrogen ions in aqueous solution, producing oxides or salts. [[Rust|Rusting]], the formation of red-orange [[Iron]] oxides, is the most familiar example. Corrosion can form pits or cracks or spread across a surface, and because it is a [[Diffusion|diffusion]]-controlled process it occurs on exposed surfaces. In galvanic corrosion, two different metals in electrical contact within an electrolyte cause the more active metal, the anode, to corrode faster. [[Zinc]] is often used as a sacrificial anode for steel structures. Corrosion costs approximately $2.5 trillion globally each year in maintenance and replacement. Prevention includes protective [[Paint]] and chromium alloying to form passive oxide layers, as in [[Stainless steel]].

Dishonest or fraudulent conduct by those in positions of authority, for illicit personal gain. Corruption includes [[Fraud|fraud]], bribery, influence peddling and embezzlement, as well as some practices that are legal in many countries, such as lobbying. Political corruption occurs when an office-holder or other governmental employee acts in an official capacity for personal gain. Historically the term had a broader moral meaning: the ancient Greek philosopher [[Socrates]] was condemned to death partly for "corrupting the young." Corruption is perceived as most common in kleptocracies, oligarchies, narco-states and authoritarian states, but it also occurs in wealthy capitalist economies. Critics argue that global measures such as the Corruption Perceptions Index mostly survey executives about bribery and under-measure the legalized corruption of the rich. Strategies against corruption are grouped under anti-corruption, and the [[United Nations]] Sustainable Development Goal 16 aims to reduce it substantially.

[[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] island and territorial collectivity of [[France]] (pop., 2026: 365,636). The fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean, Corsica lies southeast of the French mainland and immediately north of [[Sardinia]]. A single mountain chain covers two-thirds of the island. The [[Republic of Genoa]] ruled it from 1284 to 1755. In 1768 Genoa ceded it to [[Louis XV]] in return for debts incurred after French help in suppressing a Corsican revolt. [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]], later emperor of the French, was born in Ajaccio in 1769. After an armed standoff with French authorities in 1975, a conflict between French forces and nationalist groups, notably the National Liberation Front of Corsica (FLNC), continued until a truce with its largest faction in 2014. Violence resumed after the 2022 murder of the jailed nationalist Yvan Colonna, and in 2023 two FLNC factions resumed armed conflict.

Glucocorticoid [[Steroid|steroid]] hormone, known as a [[Stress (biology)|stress]] hormone. Cortisol is produced mainly by the *zona fasciculata* of the [[Adrenal gland|adrenal cortex]], and in lower quantities in other tissues. It is released on a daily cycle and rises in response to stress and low [[Glucose|blood-glucose]] concentration. It increases blood sugar through gluconeogenesis, suppresses the [[Immune system|immune system]], aids energy [[Metabolism|metabolism]] and decreases bone formation. It acts by binding to glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid receptors inside cells, which then affect gene expression. As a medication it is known as hydrocortisone.

Crystalline form of aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃, and a [[Mineral|rock-forming mineral]]. Pure corundum is transparent, and trace impurities color it: chromium makes [[Ruby]] red, while [[Sapphire]] takes other colors from transition metals. Corundum rates 9.0 on the [[Mohs scale]], so it can scratch almost all other minerals. Emery, a black granular form mixed with [[Magnetite]] or [[Hematite]], is used as an [[Abrasive]] on sandpaper and machining tools. Its density of 4.02 g/cm³ is unusually high for a transparent mineral of light elements.

Small [[Warship|warship]], traditionally the smallest class of vessel rated as a warship. It ranks above the sloop-of-war and below the [[Frigate|frigate]]. Modern corvettes serve as coastal patrol craft, missile boats and fast attack craft, typically displacing 500 to 2,000 tons, though recent designs may approach 3,000 tons. Unlike frigates, they lack the endurance for long voyages. The rank of corvette captain, the most junior of three captain ranks in several European and South American navies, derives from the name of the ship type.

Family of cosmopolitan [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, including crows, ravens, rooks, magpies, jays and nutcrackers. Its 135 species include the [[Corvus|crows and ravens]] of the genus Corvus, which makes up over a third of the family. The [[Common raven|common raven]] is the largest passerine bird. Corvids are among the most intelligent birds studied: [[Eurasian magpie|Eurasian magpies]] have shown self-awareness in mirror tests, and crows and rooks make tools. Their brain-to-body mass ratio equals that of non-human great apes and [[Cetacean|cetaceans]]. Corvids are found worldwide except the southern tip of South America and the polar ice caps, with most species in tropical South and Central America and southern Asia. Several raven species have reached oceanic islands, and some are now threatened or extinct.

Genus of [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, including crows, ravens and rooks, in the family [[Corvidae]]. The genus name is Latin for "raven." It has about 46 species on all continents except South America, Antarctica and several islands, and makes up a third of the family. Its members appear to have evolved in Asia. The species commonly encountered in [[Europe]] are the carrion crow, hooded crow, common raven and rook. A 2002 study found that some crow species make [[Tool|tools]] as well as use them. Crows are considered among the most intelligent animals, with an encephalization quotient equal to that of many non-human primates. A group of crows is called a "flock" or a "murder."

Italian banker and politician, de facto ruler of [[Florence]]. Cosimo di Giovanni de' Medici built his power on banking wealth and intermarriage with other rich and powerful families, and he was the first to make the Medici family the effective leaders of Florence for generations. He assumed de facto control of the Florentine Republic in 1434, after a brief exile, and directed its affairs for three decades. His power was not absolute: Florence's councils resisted his proposals, and fellow politicians viewed him as first among equals rather than an autocrat. He spent over 600,000 gold florins on art and culture, including [[Donatello]]'s *David*, the first freestanding nude male sculpture since antiquity. A patron of learning and architecture, he helped make Florence a center of the [[Renaissance]]. Posthumously honored as *Pater Patriae*.

Substances applied to the body to cleanse, beautify or change appearance, or to add fragrance. Cosmetics are [[Mixture|mixtures]] of [[Chemical compound|chemical compounds]] from natural or synthetic sources, used for skin care, [[Perfume|fragrance]], hair coloring and makeup. People have used them for thousands of years; in Mesopotamia and Egypt, minerals such as galena and malachite were ground into [[Pigment|pigments]] for eye enhancement as early as 4000 BC. Early cosmetics often contained [[Lead|lead]], which caused serious illness and sometimes death. Modern products are generally tested for safety but may contain controversial ingredients such as [[PFAS]] and [[Formaldehyde]] releasers. In the United States, cosmetics do not require approval from the Food and Drug Administration before marketing, although products are monitored. The [[European Union]] has banned animal testing for finished cosmetic products since 2004 and for ingredients since 2013.

Succession of methods by which astronomers determine distances to celestial objects. Also called the extragalactic distance scale, the ladder is needed because no single method works at all ranges. Direct measurement works only within about 1,000 [[Parsec|parsecs]]. Each rung calibrates the next: [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid variables]] calibrate distances to the [[Large Magellanic Cloud]], and [[Supernova|Type Ia supernovae]] extend measurements to distant galaxies. Combining supernova distances with [[Redshift|redshift]] data gives Hubble constant values of 73–75 km/s/Mpc, while cosmic microwave background data give about 67 km/s/Mpc, a discrepancy known as the Hubble tension. Precision is about 1% at the nearest anchors and degrades to 5–10% at cosmological scales.

Theory of exponential expansion of space in the very early [[Universe|universe]]. This expansion supercooled the universe and ended when the energy of the driving [[Field (physics)|field]] condensed into hot, dense particles, a process called reheating. Inflation theory was developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s by, among others, Alexei Starobinsky, Alan Guth and Andrei Linde, who shared the 2014 Kavli Prize. Quantum fluctuations in the inflationary region, magnified to cosmic size, became the seeds of cosmic structure. Many physicists believe inflation explains why the universe is isotropic and flat and why no magnetic monopoles have been observed. Temperature variations measured by the COBE satellite in 1992 agree with its predictions, although the [[Particle physics|particle physics]] mechanism remains unknown and some scientists dissent.

[[Microwave]] radiation that fills the [[Observable universe|observable universe]], a relic of the [[Big Bang]]. Its energy density exceeds that of all the photons emitted by all the stars in history. American radio astronomers Arno Penzias and Robert Woodrow Wilson discovered it by accident, and it is key evidence for the Big Bang theory. As the universe expanded, protons and electrons combined into neutral atoms in the recombination epoch, and [[Photon|photons]] began to travel freely; their wavelengths have since stretched through [[Redshift|cosmological redshift]]. The background is very uniform, but sensitive detectors measure temperature variations of about one part in 100,000. Its power spectrum reveals the density of normal and [[Dark matter|dark matter]]. Satellites including COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped it, and COBE work earned John Mather and George Smoot the 2006 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] in Physics.

High-energy [[Proton|proton]] or atomic nucleus moving at nearly the speed of light. Cosmic rays come from the Milky Way, from distant galaxies and from the Sun. Victor Hess discovered them in 1912 with balloon experiments that showed radiation increasing with altitude, and he received the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics. Protons make up about 89% of primary cosmic rays, with helium nuclei about 10%. On striking the atmosphere they produce showers of secondary particles, but most are deflected into space by [[Earth's magnetic field|Earth's magnetic field]] or the [[Heliosphere]]. Neutrinos and gamma rays from the [[Blazar|blazar]] TXS 0506+056 in 2018 suggest that active galactic nuclei also produce cosmic rays, and Fermi Space Telescope data have been interpreted as evidence that many originate from [[Supernova|supernova]] explosions.

Coefficient in the field equations of [[General relativity|general relativity]] representing the energy density of empty space. [[Albert Einstein]] introduced it in 1917 to counterbalance gravity and produce a static universe, then abandoned it after [[Edwin Hubble]] confirmed that the universe was expanding. Most physicists took it to be zero from the 1930s until 1998, when the discovery that expansion is accelerating suggested a positive value. Denoted Λ, it is the simplest explanation for [[Dark energy|dark energy]], which makes up about 68% of the universe's mass–energy density in the ΛCDM model. [[Quantum field theory|Quantum field theory]], however, predicts a [[Vacuum|vacuum]] energy exceeding the observed value by some 120 orders of magnitude, a discrepancy called the cosmological constant problem.

Study of the universe as a whole, including its origin, structure and ultimate fate. Physical cosmology, a sub-branch of [[Astronomy|astronomy]], examines the chronology of the universe, its large-scale structure and dynamics. Modern physical cosmology is dominated by the [[Big Bang]] theory in the ΛCDM model, which includes [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and [[Dark energy|dark energy]]. The field overlaps [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]] and philosophy, so its theories may include untestable assumptions. Earlier religious and mythological cosmologies rested on [[Creation myth|creation myths]] and [[Eschatology|eschatology]].

Cossack state in central [[Ukraine]], 1648–1764. Established by Registered [[Cossacks]] under [[Bohdan Khmelnytsky]] during the Khmelnytsky Uprising, it was officially the Zaporozhian Host and covered mostly central Ukraine, with parts of [[Belarus]] and southwestern Russia. The [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] recognized it by the Treaty of Zboriv in 1649. The Treaty of Pereiaslav in 1654 established vassal relations with the Tsardom of [[Moscow]], a benchmark in Soviet, Ukrainian and Russian historiography. The 1667 Treaty of Andrusovo, made without Cossack representation, divided the Hetmanate along the [[Dnieper]]. After Ivan Mazepa's failed attempt to break with Russia in 1708, Cossack autonomy was severely restricted. Catherine II abolished the office of hetman in 1764, and the last remnants of its administration ended in 1781. Descendants of its ruling class pioneered the Ukrainian national revival of the 19th century.

Predominantly East Slavic, Eastern Orthodox military people of the [[Steppe|steppe]] of eastern Ukraine and southern Russia. Cossacks defended the southern borders of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] and the [[Russian Empire]] against Crimean–Nogai raids, in return for privileges and considerable self-governance. Their groups were organized into autonomous hosts. The Zaporozhian Cossacks were mostly infantry who used war wagons, while the Don Cossacks were primarily [[Cavalry|cavalry]], an important development in mounted warfare. The [[Russian Revolution]] disrupted Cossack society, and after World War II the Soviet Union disbanded Cossack units. In 1988, however, it permitted the re-establishment of former hosts. Between 3.5 and 5 million people identify with Cossack culture, though most have little connection with the original people. Cossack organizations operate in Russia, Ukraine, [[Belarus]], [[Kazakhstan]], Canada and the United States.

Country in [[Central America]], officially the Republic of Costa Rica. It borders [[Nicaragua]] to the north, [[Panama]] to the southeast, the [[Caribbean Sea]] to the northeast and the [[Pacific Ocean]] to the southwest. Its land area is nearly 51,180 sq km, and its population is around five million, with about 350,000 living in the capital, San José. Humans have been present since 7,000–10,000 BC. A peripheral colony of the [[Spanish Empire]] until 1821, Costa Rica joined the Federal Republic of Central America in 1823 and formally declared independence in 1847. After a brief civil war in 1948, the 1949 constitution abolished the army, so Costa Rica is one of the few sovereign nations without a standing military. Education has been free and compulsory since 1886. Costa Rica ranked 62nd in the [[Human Development Index]] in 2023 and is the only [[OECD]] country in Central America and the Caribbean.
